items.title: CGI Foundations
items.description: The shared starting point for every DART pathway: the concepts and workflows of computer-generated imagery, from modeling and texturing to lighting, camera and rendering, practiced on two subjects and brought together in a final project.

oerFields.estimatedDuration: One course run (6 or 15 weeks, same credits)
learningObjectives: Understand the fundamental principles of computer-generated imagery (CGI) and its applications
Develop proficiency in using basic 3D modeling tools and techniques
Gain knowledge of the essential elements of 3D rendering, including lighting, shading, and texturing
Learn to create and manipulate 3D assets, including characters, environments, and props
Explore the pipeline and workflow of a typical CGI project from concept to final output
Analyze the history and evolution of CGI in various industries such as film, gaming, and advertising
testOutCriteria: Polygonal models have good edge flow
UVs are clearly laid out and well packed
Scene is well lit using scene lights or emissive materials
B+ or better on all lecture quizzes
oerFields.whoItsFor: Everyone starting out in 3D. Take it as DART 203, or in your first run of DART 303 if you have not taken DART 203.

items.description: Creates animated graphics for multimedia projects, often involving typography and visual effects.

items.title: Physically Based
items.description: A database of physically based values for CG artists

items.title: 7 Tips to Make a More Realistic Rendering
items.description: Rendering guide

items.title: Universal Everything
items.description: A collective of media artists, experience designers and future makers.

items.title: Cradle to Cradle: Remaking the Way We Make Things
Adam Curtis and the Secret History of Everything
Dilemmas in a General Theory of Planning
How to Make Almost Anything: The Digital Fabrication Revolution
items.description: The accessible statement of the fab-lab thesis: personal fabrication as the next computing revolution. Sets up the course's central question — what changes when anyone can make (almost) anything?

items.title: Fab: The Coming Revolution on Your Desktop
items.description: Recommended background for; the origin of the fab-lab network.

items.title: The Nature and Art of Workmanship — the workmanship of risk and of certainty
items.description: The sharpest available frame for what a machine takes over and what it leaves to the maker. Returns in week 5 when students have felt it on the laser.

items.title: Abstracting Craft: The Practiced Digital Hand — ch. 1, Hands
items.description: Argues that digital work can be craft; pairs with Pye for the Project 1 crit week.

items.title: The Craftsman — Prologue: Man as His Own Maker
items.description: Recommended: craft as the desire to do a job well for its own sake; useful vocabulary for crit.

items.title: Digital Fabrications: Architectural and Material Techniques — Introduction; Sectioning; Folding
items.description: Organizes digital fabrication by technique family (sectioning, tessellating, folding, contouring, forming) with built examples — the vocabulary for sheet-to-form.

items.title: Design for 3D printing — knowledge base
items.description: Practical FDM design rules (wall thickness, overhangs, tolerances); the reference for and the checklist.

oerFields.publisher: How to design parts for FDM

items.title: Prusa Knowledge Base — print quality troubleshooting and slicing basics
items.description: Recommended: diagnosing failed prints; replace with the shop's own slicer documentation once known.

items.title: The Alphabet and the Algorithm — ch. 1, Variable, Identical, Differential
items.description: The theory of the digital multiple: identical copies vs. variable families; the intellectual core of Project 2.

items.title: Form+Code in Design, Art, and Architecture — Parameterize
items.description: Recommended: parametric thinking with art/design examples; a bridge from the program's code-based work to fabrication.

items.title: Digital Handmade: Craftsmanship and the New Industrial Revolution
items.description: Recommended precedent source: makers and studios combining digital fabrication with craft; good for finding Project 2 examples.

oerFields.publisher: Craftsmanship in the New Industrial Revolution

items.title: Critical Making: Conceptual and Material Studies in Technology and Social Life
items.description: Defines critical making — making as a way of thinking critically about technology; frames the final project.

items.title: Making It: Pick up a spot welder and join the revolution
items.description: The sharpest popular critique of the maker movement; discussed against Gershenfeld and Anderson.

oerFields.publisher: Pick up a spot welder and join the revolution

items.title: Makers: The New Industrial Revolution — ch. 1
items.description: Recommended as the foil for: the boosterish version of the maker thesis.

items.title: Materials against materiality
items.description: Recommended: attention to materials as processes rather than properties; useful for the finishing and hybrid-process week.

items.title: Thinking Through Craft — Introduction
items.description: Recommended: craft as a set of positions (supplemental, material, skilled, pastoral, amateur) rather than a category of objects.

items.title: Shaping Things
items.description: Recommended: spimes — objects that carry their data and history; relevant to file-as-publication and the theme.

items.title: Fab Academy — How to Make (Almost) Anything class archive
items.description: Reference: the global fab-lab curriculum with weekly process pages; a source for demos and a model for documentation.

items.title: Nervous System — studio project pages
items.description: Reference precedent for generative multiples across printing, cutting, and casting. Also cited on slide 9 (Kinematics Dress, 2014) as the course's first additive example — students meet the studio on day one and return to it in.

items.title: The 3D Additivist Manifesto
items.description: Short, open, 3D-printing-specific, and deliberately provocative — the counterweight to the design-guide readings in the print week; returns in as a critical-making text. Assigned at UNT.

items.title: Product design
items.description: Designs consumer products in 3D for manufacturing or visualization purposes.

items.title: Pathways

items.title: Production management
items.description: Oversees the planning and execution of 3D projects, ensuring deadlines and budgets are met.

items.title: Short Film and VFX Pathway
items.description: A comprehensive pathway for creating animated short films with visual effects. This pathway combines traditional animation techniques with advanced simulation and compositing skills to produce cinematic CGI content with professional VFX elements.

learningObjectives: Create complete animated short films from concept to final render
Integrate realistic visual effects with animated content
Apply professional compositing workflows to enhance final output
Understand the full pipeline from pre-production to post-production

items.title: Short Film Pathway
items.description: Create compelling animated short films from concept to final render. This pathway covers the essential skills for producing narrative-driven CGI films with professional quality animation and compositing.

learningObjectives: Develop strong storytelling and narrative skills for animation
Create character performances that convey emotion and personality
Produce complete animated short films from concept to completion
Apply professional compositing and finishing techniques
Understand animation production pipelines and workflows

items.title: Object autopsy
items.description: Choose a manufactured object you own.

items.title: Laser material test + kerf swatch
items.description: Cut a material test grid (power × speed) and a kerf comb in one sheet material.

items.title: Press-fit construction kit
items.description: Design a kit of no more than three part types that press-fit into at least two different structures.

items.title: Print iteration: one object, three revisions
items.description: Design a small object with a fit (a lid, a snap, a hinge) and print it three times, changing one thing each time in response to what failed.

items.title: Parametric family
items.description: Build a parametric model with at least three exposed parameters and generate a family of five variants.

items.title: CNC relief tile
items.description: Design a 2.5D relief tile from a heightmap or modeled surface, set up the CAM job, and have it cut.

items.title: Documentation portfolio
items.description: A single site or PDF documenting every exercise and project: photographs, files, settings, failures, and what you would do differently.

items.title: Reading responses
items.description: For each required reading, a 200–300-word response that connects one idea in the text to something you made or saw in the shop that week.

items.title: Critique participation
items.description: Prepared, specific, and generous participation in the four crits, following the protocol.

items.title: Precedent presentation
items.description: Each student presents one artist, designer, or studio and one specific work made with digital fabrication: how it was made (process, machine, material), why that process, and what it argues.

items.title: Project 1: Sheet to form
items.description: Make a three-dimensional object from flat sheet material using sectioning, folding, or joinery, responding to the theme.

items.title: Project 2: Multiples and variation
items.description: Produce a series of at least five objects in which variation is designed — parametric, generative, or rule-based — and the series says something the single object cannot.

items.title: Final project
items.description: A self-directed project answering one of the selected themes, using at least two fabrication processes, developed through the proposal, a work-in-progress crit, and a final exhibition.
